pages.text: The old stone house in Abha had stood empty for almost a decade, and by the time Lina pushed open its heavy wooden door, the smell of dust and damp rushed out to greet her like an impatient relative. Her uncle Mansour was already inside, clipboard in hand, measuring cracks with the grim satisfaction of a man who had been proved right. "The roof leaks, the walls are crumbling, and the electrics are older than your father," he announced, without looking up. "The builders start on Thursday, and frankly, not a moment too soon." Lina barely heard him, because her eyes had drifted to the far wall of the majlis. Even beneath a veil of grime, it blazed with colour: bands of crimson, ochre and deep green, triangles nested inside diamonds, lines of white dots marching across the plaster like tiny soldiers. She had seen photographs of Al-Qatt Al-Asiri in school, but standing in front of the real thing, painted by her own great-grandmother Hessa, took her breath away.

As she stepped closer, Lina noticed something odd about the pattern. Every panel was crowded with shapes and colour, except one in the lower right corner, which had been left almost entirely bare. Squinting, she could just make out faint charcoal lines sketched across it, as though someone had planned a design and then simply walked away. "Uncle, what happens to this wall?" she asked, trying to keep her voice casual. Mansour finally glanced up, and his expression softened for a moment before hardening again. "It's beautiful, I know, but the plaster is coming away in places, and damp is getting in behind it. We'll have to cover it with fresh cement, or the whole room will rot."

The following afternoon, a sleek car pulled up outside, and a man in a crisp white thobe introduced himself as Mr. Kassab, the owner of a gallery in Jeddah. He walked along the painted wall slowly, nodding as if he were doing sums in his head, which, Lina suspected, he was. "Collectors would pay a great deal for authentic panels like these," he said smoothly. "My team can cut them out in sections, frame them, and sell them on your behalf, and the money would more than cover your repairs." Uncle Mansour rubbed his chin, clearly tempted, and Lina felt her stomach drop. The thought of her great-grandmother's work hanging in pieces in strangers' homes, separated like the pages of a torn book, struck her as nothing short of a betrayal. "Give me until Thursday," Mansour said at last, and Mr. Kassab smiled the patient smile of someone who rarely lost a deal.

That evening, Lina persuaded her older brother Faris to walk with her to the house of Umm Saeed, an elderly neighbour who, according to family legend, had painted walls all over the village in her youth. They found her on her terrace, wrapped in a shawl, pouring cardamom coffee into tiny cups. When Lina described the bare panel, the old woman set down the pot and laughed softly, her eyes glistening. "So she never told any of you," she murmured. "Hessa and I painted that majlis together, the year your grandfather was born, and she refused to let me fill that corner." Lina leaned forward, hardly daring to breathe.

"In those days, the women of the house painted the walls before every Eid and every wedding," Umm Saeed explained, tracing a triangle in the air with one wrinkled finger. "Hessa used to say that a wall is never truly finished while a family still lives behind it. She left that space for whoever came next, a daughter, a granddaughter, anyone with the patience to learn." Faris raised his eyebrows at his sister, who had gone very quiet. "And the charcoal lines?" Lina asked eventually. "Just a suggestion," the old woman replied, with a mischievous shrug. "She always said the next painter should feel free to ignore her completely."

Umm Saeed's expression darkened, however, when Lina mentioned Mr. Kassab's offer. "Cut them out?" she repeated, horrified. "These walls are mud and stone, child, not canvas; the moment a saw touches them, the plaster will shatter like glass." Lina's mind began racing, and by the time she and Faris got home, she had already drawn up a plan. She spent half the night reading articles on heritage conservation, watching interviews with restorers, and taking careful photographs of every crack in the majlis. She even discovered that Al-Qatt Al-Asiri had been recognised by UNESCO as part of humanity's cultural heritage, which made the idea of selling it off in chunks seem even more absurd. By dawn, her eyes were bloodshot, but she had a proposal that, she hoped, even her practical uncle couldn't dismiss out of hand.

Rather than wait for permission, Lina decided to prove the wall could be saved. For three nights, Umm Saeed taught her how to clean the old paint with nothing harsher than soft brushes and patience, and how to mix colours the way they had once been mixed, though nowadays they used modern pigments alongside the traditional ones. Faris, who claimed to have no artistic talent whatsoever, held the lamp and offered unhelpful commentary, yet never once suggested going to bed. Lina made countless mistakes: a line that wobbled, a green that dried far too dark, a dot that turned stubbornly into a smudge. Each time, Umm Saeed simply handed her a damp cloth and said, "Again." Slowly, as the grime lifted, the old colours began to glow, and the wall seemed to wake from a very long sleep.

On Thursday morning, Mr. Kassab arrived with two workmen and an electric saw, and Uncle Mansour followed them into the majlis, looking tired and resigned. He stopped dead in the doorway. One whole section of the wall, freshly cleaned, now shone as brilliantly as it must have done seventy years earlier, and in its centre, previously hidden beneath dirt, a delicate pattern of interlocking lines spelled out a single name: Hessa. "She signed it," Mansour whispered, his clipboard hanging forgotten at his side. Lina stepped forward and, with a voice steadier than she felt, explained what Umm Saeed had told her about the fragile plaster, showing him photographs, articles and a rough estimate she had made of what it would actually cost to repair the leaking roof. Mr. Kassab cleared his throat impatiently, but nobody was paying him the slightest attention.

For a long moment, Uncle Mansour said nothing at all. Then he turned to the gallery owner and, with impeccable politeness, thanked him for his time and showed him to the door. "I've been so focused on what this house was costing us," he admitted afterwards, "that I completely lost sight of what it's worth." Within days, the whole family had rolled up their sleeves: cousins carried tiles up ladders, Faris discovered a surprising talent for fixing gutters, and a conservation specialist from the regional heritage office came to advise on sealing the damp. The builders still came, but this time they repaired the roof instead of plastering over the past. Umm Saeed supervised everything from a plastic chair in the courtyard, issuing instructions like a general commanding her troops.

On the eve of Eid, with the house full of relatives and the scent of incense drifting through the rooms, Lina finally knelt before the empty corner of the wall. She had studied Hessa's charcoal lines for weeks, and in the end she kept some and boldly ignored others, just as her great-grandmother had invited her to. She painted a band of the deep green Hessa had loved, framed it with crimson triangles, and, at its heart, wove her own name into the pattern so subtly that only someone who knew where to look would ever find it. When she stepped back, the room fell silent, and then Umm Saeed began to clap, and soon everyone had joined in. Yet Lina had done one more thing that nobody noticed until much later: in the very corner of her panel, she had left a small space untouched. After all, she thought with a smile, a wall is never truly finished while a family still lives behind it.

stories.title: The Girl Who Finished the Star

pages.text: Huda had made up her mind, long before the car turned into the narrow lanes of Al-Balad, that this was going to be the dullest weekend of her life. Her family had spent months restoring Bayt al-Nour, the crumbling coral-stone house in old Jeddah where her grandmother had grown up, and every visit seemed to involve dust, heat and endless conversations about wooden beams. "You could at least pretend to be interested," her older brother muttered as they climbed out into the humid afternoon. Huda rolled her eyes, though she couldn't help glancing up at the enormous wooden roshan that jutted out from the first floor, its lattice of interlocking stars throwing delicate shadows onto the street. She had walked past that window a hundred times without really looking at it. Her grandmother, leaning on her stick in the doorway, smiled as if she knew something Huda didn't.

"I need someone with young eyes to sort out the storeroom on the top floor," her grandmother announced, and before Huda could come up with an excuse, she found herself climbing a staircase that creaked in protest at every step. The storeroom was crammed with chests, rolled-up carpets and boxes that hadn't been opened for decades. Wedged behind a cracked mirror, she discovered a bundle wrapped in faded green cloth. Inside lay a brass astrolabe, its surface engraved with tiny Arabic letters and the names of stars, together with a scrap of paper on which someone had written in careful handwriting: "Turn it only towards the evening star, and return before it sets." Huda assumed it was some kind of family joke, yet her fingers were trembling slightly as she rotated the delicate inner disc. The moment the pointer settled on the star marked Al-Zuhara, a warm wind that smelled unmistakably of salt swept through the windowless room.

When the dizziness faded, the first thing Huda noticed was the silence where the hum of air conditioners should have been. She was standing in the same storeroom, but it was almost empty, and through a gap in the shutters she could see the masts of wooden dhows rocking in a harbour that seemed impossibly close. Somewhere below, the call to prayer drifted over rooftops that had no satellite dishes, and a man was leading a heavily loaded camel through the lane. "Who are you, and what on earth are you wearing?" demanded a voice behind her. Huda spun round to face a girl of about her own age, dressed in a long embroidered dress, clutching a battered notebook to her chest. Thinking on her feet, Huda claimed she was a cousin visiting from Makkah, and to her astonishment, the girl, whose name was Fatimah, seemed to accept the story without a second thought.

It didn't take long for Huda to work out that she had landed somewhere in the 1940s, nor to realise, with a jolt, that Fatimah's family name was the same as her own. Over glasses of sweet mint tea in the courtyard, Fatimah explained that her father, a carpenter, had been commissioned to build a new roshan for the front of the house. "I've been designing patterns for it for months," she confided, opening her notebook to reveal pages covered in intricate geometric sketches. "But the master carpenter says a girl's drawings belong in the kitchen fire, and my father won't go against him unless the design is perfect." She traced the central motif with her finger, an elaborate star that simply refused to close properly at its edges. "If I can't solve it by tomorrow morning, I'm going to give up for good."

Huda stared at the half-finished pattern, and a shiver ran down her spine, because she had seen it only hours earlier, carved in wood above the street. The star that Fatimah couldn't complete was the very one in the window she had dismissed as old-fashioned on her way in. "The problem isn't your idea," she said slowly, "it's the angles; you're trying to fit eight points into a circle without dividing it evenly first." She borrowed a piece of string and a nail, and, drawing on a geometry lesson she had barely paid attention to the previous term, showed Fatimah how to construct perfect divisions using nothing but a fixed point and a steady hand. Fatimah's eyes widened as the lines began to fall into place, each one locking neatly into the next like pieces of a puzzle. For the first time in her life, Huda understood that maths could be beautiful.

They worked late into the evening by the flickering light of an oil lamp, arguing cheerfully over curves and spacing, and laughing whenever the ink smudged. Every so often, Huda glanced anxiously at the astrolabe hidden in the folds of her abaya, where the pointer was creeping steadily towards the horizon line. She had no idea what would happen if the evening star set while she was still here, and she certainly didn't intend to find out the hard way. Yet she couldn't bring herself to leave before the design was finished, not when Fatimah was humming happily beside her, more confident with every stroke of the pen. "You've got a gift for this, you know," Huda said quietly, and she meant every word. Fatimah looked up, startled, as though nobody had ever told her so before.

Just as the last line was drawn, Fatimah's father stepped into the courtyard, wiping sawdust from his hands. He studied the drawing for a long time without speaking, while both girls held their breath. "Who taught you to divide the circle like this?" he finally asked his daughter, and Fatimah, after a quick glance at Huda, answered that a friend had shown her the method, but the pattern itself was entirely her own. Her father nodded slowly, a smile tugging at the corners of his mouth. "Then the master carpenter will have to eat his words, because this is the design we'll use," he declared. Fatimah let out a cry of delight, and in the excitement nobody noticed Huda slipping quietly up the stairs.

At the top of the staircase, Fatimah caught up with her, breathless and puzzled. "You're not really from Makkah, are you?" she asked, and Huda, unable to lie to her a second time, simply shook her head. Fatimah considered this for a moment, then pressed something into her hand: a small pencil sketch of the finished star, signed with her name in neat, determined letters. "Wherever you're going, take this so you don't forget me," she said. Huda swallowed the lump in her throat and promised that she never would. Then, with the evening star trembling on the very edge of the horizon, she turned the brass disc back to where it had started.

She found herself sprawled on the dusty floor of the crowded storeroom, with the noise of traffic and air conditioners rushing back into her ears. According to her phone, barely a minute had passed, yet the sketch was still clutched tightly in her fist, the paper yellow and brittle with age. Huda hurried downstairs and out into the street, where she stood gazing up at the roshan as though seeing it for the first time. Every line of the star was exactly as she and Fatimah had drawn it by lamplight. "Your great-grandmother designed that, you know," her grandmother said, appearing beside her. "She used to tell us that a mysterious guest helped her finish it, a girl with the strangest shoes anyone had ever seen."

Huda looked down at her trainers and burst out laughing, while her grandmother raised a curious eyebrow but, wisely, asked no questions. For the rest of the weekend, nobody could drag her away from the restoration work, and her brother joked that she had been replaced by an entirely different person. In a sense, she supposed, she had. That evening she carefully placed the sketch inside a frame and hung it in the room where she and Fatimah had worked together, decades apart and yet side by side. Before she fell asleep, she opened a new notebook and wrote on the first page, in neat and determined letters: "Future architect." Somewhere, she felt sure, a girl in an embroidered dress would have approved.

pages.text: Faisal had always considered his grandfather's stories charming but hopelessly out of date, like a cassette tape in a world of streaming. So when Jaddi Saad announced, over Friday lunch, that he intended to find the old well where his own father had once watered camels, Faisal barely looked up from his phone. 'Nobody navigates by memory anymore, Jaddi,' he said, with the easy confidence of a sixteen-year-old who had never been truly lost. His sister Noura, who was a year older and never went anywhere without her camera, kicked him under the table. Their grandfather merely smiled and unfolded a piece of yellowed paper covered in faded ink. 'This map has no roads on it,' he said quietly, 'because when it was drawn, there were none.'

They set off before dawn three days later, the old Land Cruiser loaded with water, dates and enough blankets to survive a winter on a mountaintop. The red dunes of the Nafud rose around them like frozen waves, their crests glowing as the sun crept over the horizon. Faisal had the route saved on a GPS device, which he consulted every few minutes with obvious satisfaction. Jaddi Saad, by contrast, kept glancing at the sky and at the shapes of distant rocks, as though reading a book that only he could see. On the hand-drawn map, the well was marked by a small circle beside a sketch of a rock shaped like a camel's head. 'If the sand hasn't swallowed it,' their grandfather murmured, 'we'll be drinking from it by sunset.'

The storm came out of nowhere, or at least that was how it seemed to Faisal. One moment the sky was a flawless blue; the next, a brown wall was rolling towards them, devouring the dunes one by one. Jaddi Saad pulled over at once, turned the car away from the wind and told them to cover their faces. For almost an hour, sand hissed against the windows like rain made of glass, and the world shrank to the inside of the vehicle. When the wind finally died down, the Land Cruiser was buried up to its wheels, the GPS screen had gone completely black, and Faisal's phone showed not a single bar of signal. Worse still, one of the water containers had split open where a loose toolbox had crashed into it.

Digging the car out proved to be harder than any of them had anticipated. Halfway through, Jaddi Saad stepped awkwardly into a hollow in the sand, and his ankle twisted beneath him with a sickening crack. Noura wrapped it tightly with a scarf while Faisal tried, and failed, to hide his panic. They took stock of their situation: one remaining container of water, an injured grandfather, and a car that was going nowhere. 'Normally, the golden rule is to stay with the vehicle,' Jaddi Saad said, his face pale but calm. 'But with this little water, waiting could cost us dearly, and the well is no more than fifteen kilometres to the east, where herders camp at this time of year.'

It was decided that Noura would stay with their grandfather in the shade of the car, while Faisal would walk to the well once the sun had set and the heat had eased. As darkness fell, Jaddi Saad pointed to a faint, steady star low in the northern sky. 'That is Al-Jadi,' he said. 'Every other star circles around it, but it never moves, which is why travellers have trusted it for a thousand years.' He explained that if Faisal kept Al-Jadi over his left shoulder, he would be heading east, towards the rock shaped like a camel's head. Faisal repeated the instructions until he could have recited them in his sleep. For the first time in his life, he found himself hanging on his grandfather's every word.

The desert at night was nothing like Faisal had imagined. The silence was so complete that he could hear his own heartbeat, and every shadow seemed to shift when he wasn't looking. More than once, he became convinced that he had drifted off course, and each time he forced himself to stop, breathe, and find Al-Jadi again. Had he been alone with only his own thoughts, he might well have given up. Instead, he kept hearing his grandfather's voice: 'Don't argue with the sky, Faisal; it has been right far longer than you have.' Hour after hour, he trudged over dunes that all looked identical, sipping his water sparingly and counting his steps to keep his mind from wandering.

By the time the eastern sky began to turn pink, Faisal's legs were trembling with exhaustion. Then, as the light grew stronger, he saw it: a dark outcrop of rock with a long neck and a blunt nose, unmistakably the camel's head from the map. A wave of relief swept over him, only to be replaced by dismay, because there was no sign of any well. He circled the rock twice, his heart sinking further with every step. It was then that he noticed fresh camel tracks pressed into the sand, all heading in the same direction around a low ridge. Mustering his last reserves of energy, he followed them.

Beyond the ridge lay a stone-lined well, a cluster of tents and a herd of camels drinking noisily from a trough. An elderly man in a brown cloak looked up in astonishment as Faisal stumbled towards him, dusty and barely able to speak. Within minutes, Faisal was sitting on a rug with a cup of water in one hand and a glass of sweet tea in the other. When he mentioned his grandfather's name, the old man's eyes widened. 'Saad bin Mansour? We were boys together at this very well, more than sixty years ago!' he exclaimed. Before Faisal had even finished his tea, the man's sons were loading a pickup truck with water and a first-aid kit.

They found the Land Cruiser easily, partly because Noura had been flashing sunlight towards the horizon with her makeup mirror ever since dawn. Jaddi Saad was weary and his ankle had swollen badly, but his spirits were remarkably high. When he saw his childhood friend climbing out of the truck, he laughed so hard that he had to wipe tears from his eyes. Noura threw her arms around her brother, scolding him and thanking him in the same breath. Faisal, for his part, couldn't stop grinning, though he was too tired to say much at all. Later that afternoon, Noura took a photograph of the two old men sitting side by side, which would end up framed on the wall of their family majlis.

A week later, with his grandfather's ankle in a cast, Faisal knocked on his door holding a fresh sheet of paper and a pen. 'I'd like to make a copy of your map,' he said, a little sheepishly, 'and I was hoping you could teach me the rest of the stars.' Jaddi Saad raised an eyebrow, clearly enjoying the moment, before patting the cushion beside him. Together they redrew the dunes, the camel's head rock and the well, and in the corner Faisal added a tiny star labelled Al-Jadi. His phone lay forgotten on the table, buzzing with messages he would answer later. Some maps, Faisal had come to realise, show you where to go, while others show you who you are.

pages.text: The fog rolled over the Sarawat Mountains like a living thing, swallowing the road ahead until Faisal could barely make out the edge of the cliff. His uncle Tariq drove with one hand on the wheel, apparently untroubled by the thousand-metre drop just beyond the window. ‘You’ll get used to it,’ he said, glancing at his nephew’s white knuckles. ‘By the end of the summer, you’ll be driving this road in your dreams.’ Faisal doubted it, but he kept his thoughts to himself. He had agreed to spend six weeks at his uncle’s wildlife research station largely because his parents had insisted, and partly because anything seemed better than another summer of staring at his phone in the Riyadh heat. Now, as the jagged peaks emerged from the mist, he began to suspect that he had underestimated this place.

The research station turned out to be little more than two stone buildings, a water tank and a room crammed with computers. On the very first morning, Uncle Tariq handed him a hard drive and a cup of cardamom coffee. ‘Your job,’ he explained, ‘is to go through the footage from our camera traps and log every animal you see.’ The cameras, strapped to trees and rocks across the valley, were triggered by movement, which meant that Faisal spent hours watching foxes sniffing at the lens, hyraxes sunbathing and troops of baboons squabbling over nothing in particular. ‘What exactly are we looking for?’ he asked on the third day, rubbing his tired eyes. His uncle paused, and when he answered, his voice was almost reverent: ‘The Arabian leopard. There may be fewer than two hundred left in the wild, and nobody has photographed one in this valley for eleven years.’

Faisal was beginning to think the leopard was little more than a legend when the phone rang early one morning. Uncle Tariq listened in silence, his expression darkening with every second. Four goats belonging to Abu Saleh, an elderly herder in the village below, had been found dead in their enclosure at dawn. ‘People are saying it was the leopard,’ his uncle said grimly as he hung up. ‘Some of the younger men are already talking about setting traps.’ Faisal felt a strange twist in his stomach, as though something he had only just begun to care about was already slipping out of reach. Within ten minutes, they were bouncing down the mountain track, the sun burning away the last of the mist.

Abu Saleh was a tall, weathered man whose family had herded goats on these slopes for generations. He received them with the courtesy that tradition demanded, pouring coffee and offering dates, but there was no mistaking the anger simmering beneath his calm. ‘My grandfather spoke of the leopard with respect,’ he said, ‘but respect does not feed my family.’ Several men stood nearby, arms folded, clearly unconvinced by the scientist from the city. Uncle Tariq did not argue; instead, he chose his words with great care. ‘Give us three days,’ he said. ‘If we cannot prove what did this, I will personally help you protect your animals, whatever it takes.’ After a long, uncomfortable silence, the old man nodded once.

While the adults talked, Faisal wandered over to the enclosure, where the ground was soft from recent rain. He crouched down and studied a confusion of prints pressed into the mud, remembering something his uncle had mentioned during one of their long evenings at the station. Cats, including leopards, retract their claws when they walk, so their tracks show only rounded pads; dogs, on the other hand, leave the sharp marks of their claws behind. Faisal took out his phone, placed a pen beside the clearest print for scale, and photographed it from several angles. The tiny triangular marks at the front of each toe were unmistakable. ‘Uncle,’ he called, trying to keep the excitement out of his voice, ‘I think you should take a look at this.’

The tracks were promising, but Uncle Tariq warned that a few photographs in the mud would hardly change anyone’s mind. ‘People believe what they see with their own eyes,’ he said. So that evening, armed with a thermal camera borrowed from the station, Faisal settled into a hiding place behind a low stone wall overlooking the enclosure. To his surprise, he was not alone for long: Abu Saleh’s grandson Hamad, a quiet boy of about his own age, climbed up beside him carrying a flask of tea. ‘My grandfather wants to know the truth as much as you do,’ Hamad murmured, handing him a cup. The hours crept by, and the two boys spoke in whispers about school, football and the strange silence of the mountains after dark. Somewhere in the valley, an owl called, and then the night went utterly still.

It was just after two o’clock when Hamad gripped Faisal’s arm. On the grey screen of the thermal camera, five glowing shapes were slinking down the slope towards the goats, low and purposeful. They were not cats; their ears were pointed, their tails swung loosely, and they moved together in a tight, practised group. ‘Feral dogs,’ Faisal breathed, his heart hammering against his ribs. He kept the camera steady while Hamad switched on a powerful torch and shouted at the top of his lungs. The pack scattered instantly, vanishing into the darkness with frightened yelps, and inside the enclosure the goats bleated in panic but remained unharmed. For a moment, the two boys simply stared at each other, hardly able to believe what they had witnessed.

The next afternoon, half the village crowded into Abu Saleh’s majlis to watch the footage on Faisal’s laptop. Nobody spoke as the ghostly figures of the dogs crept across the screen, and when the clip ended, a murmur of astonishment rippled through the room. Abu Saleh turned to Faisal and studied him for a long moment. ‘It seems we nearly punished an innocent creature for another’s crime,’ he admitted. ‘That would have been a great injustice, and a great shame.’ Uncle Tariq then explained that the station would help the village build stronger enclosures and work with local authorities to deal with the dog pack humanely. By the time the coffee had been served for a third time, the talk of traps had died away completely.

On his final morning, Faisal hiked up to retrieve the memory card from the most remote camera, perched high on a ridge that he had never visited before. Back at the station, he loaded the files without much expectation, half-listening to his uncle making breakfast in the next room. Then he froze. In the pale light of dawn, a female leopard was walking along the ridge, her spotted coat almost invisible against the rocks, her eyes glowing gold. Behind her, stumbling clumsily over a stone, came a single tiny cub. ‘Uncle Tariq!’ he shouted, so loudly that a cup crashed to the floor. His uncle rushed in, stared at the screen, and for the first time that summer, Faisal saw a grown man completely lost for words.

Before they left the mountains, they drove down to the village one last time to show Abu Saleh the photograph. The old man held the printed picture in his hands for a long while, tracing the outline of the cub with one rough finger. ‘My grandfather would have been happy to see this,’ he said quietly. ‘Tell me, young man, what will you do with your life now?’ Faisal hesitated, then realised that the answer had been forming inside him all summer without his noticing. ‘I think I’d like to come back,’ he said, ‘and help make sure there are still leopards here when Hamad’s grandchildren are old enough to look for them.’ As they climbed the winding road out of the valley, the fog rolled in once more, and this time Faisal did not grip the seat at all.

pages.text: Yusuf had always thought of his grandfather's house in Al-Balad as a ship that had somehow run aground in the middle of Jeddah. Its walls were built of coral stone dragged from the Red Sea a century and a half ago, and its tall wooden roshan windows leaned out over the narrow lane like curious faces. This week, however, the old house felt less like a ship and more like a museum waiting to happen. On Thursday morning, a curator from the new heritage centre was coming to collect the family's most precious possession: the pearl ledger kept by Yusuf's great-great-grandfather, a merchant who had traded with India and the Gulf. Every page recorded a voyage, a price, a name, and occasionally a storm that had nearly cost a crew their lives. Yusuf, who was sixteen and secretly proud of the whole thing, had been counting down the days.

On Tuesday morning, the ledger was gone. Yusuf's father discovered the empty space on the study desk just after Fajr, and within minutes the entire household had gathered in the doorway, speaking over one another. "It can't simply have walked away," said Uncle Faisal, running a hand over his beard. "Someone has taken it, and I don't think we need to look very far." Every head turned, almost against its will, towards the courtyard, where Hamid the carpenter was already unpacking his tools. For three weeks he had been restoring the study's roshan, carefully replacing panels that termites had hollowed out over the decades. He was the only outsider who had spent any time in that room.

Yusuf felt a knot tighten in his stomach as he watched Hamid's face change when he realised what was being implied. The carpenter put down his chisel, walked calmly to the doorway and offered to empty every bag and box he owned. "I have worked in this neighbourhood for thirty years," he said quietly, "and no family has ever had reason to count their spoons after I left." Uncle Faisal muttered something about formalities, but the damage had clearly been done. Later, Yusuf's younger sister Lina pulled him aside with the sharp expression she wore when a maths problem refused to behave. "Here's what bothers me," she whispered. "The study was locked last night, and the only key hangs on Jiddo's chain, which he never takes off."

That afternoon, while the adults argued politely in the majlis, Yusuf let himself into the study to look for himself. There was no sign of forced entry: the lock was undamaged, and Hamid's new roshan panels were firmly fixed and still smelled of fresh cedar. On the desk, a thin film of dust had settled everywhere except for a clean rectangle where the ledger had rested for years. Then he noticed something on the floor that he had walked past a hundred times without seeing. A faint trail of fine sawdust, carried from Hamid's workbench, led from the desk towards the door, pressed into the shape of footprints. They were not the marks of work boots, but of soft slippers, one of them worn noticeably flat at the heel, the way a man wears them when he drags his left foot slightly.

Yusuf knew only one person in the house who walked like that. His grandfather was eighty-seven, and over the past year his memory had begun to drift in and out like the tide, sharp one hour and clouded the next. At dinner that evening, Jiddo stared into his cup of cardamom coffee for a long time before speaking. "The water came up to the third step," he murmured, to nobody in particular. "You must keep the book dry." Uncle Faisal patted his arm gently and changed the subject, assuming the old man was lost in some distant afternoon. Yusuf, however, could not shake the feeling that his grandfather had just told them exactly where to look, if only they knew how to listen.

After dinner, Lina found Yusuf sitting on the staircase, turning the words over in his mind. "Don't you remember the story he used to tell us when we were little?" she asked, settling beside him. "The year of the great rain, when he was a boy, and the lane outside turned into a river overnight." Gradually it came back to Yusuf: how the floodwater had crept into the house, how young Jiddo had been terrified that the family's papers would be ruined, and how he had hidden something precious until the danger passed. In those days, of course, nobody had dreamed of museums; the ledger had simply been the record of how the family earned its bread. Yusuf looked down at the worn steps beneath him and felt the hairs on his arms rise.

They decided to wait until the house was asleep, partly out of curiosity and partly because neither of them wanted to raise false hopes. Shortly after midnight, a soft shuffling sound drifted down the corridor, and the two of them pressed themselves into the shadow of the stairwell. Their grandfather appeared, wrapped in his shawl, moving slowly but with surprising purpose. He paused at the bottom of the staircase, counted under his breath, and laid his palm flat against the wall beside the third step, as though reassuring himself that something was still there. Outside, rain was pattering against the roshan, an unusual sound in Jeddah, and Yusuf suddenly understood what had woken the old man's memory two nights earlier. Satisfied, Jiddo turned and shuffled back to bed without noticing his grandchildren holding their breath.

At first light, Yusuf and Lina knelt beside the third step and ran their fingers along the joints of the wall. One block of coral stone, slightly paler than its neighbours, shifted under Yusuf's thumb with a gritty whisper. Together they eased it out, and behind it lay a small, dry hollow that no one in the family had known existed. Inside, wrapped carefully in a faded cotton cloth, was the pearl ledger, completely unharmed. Beneath it lay something neither of them had expected: a folded letter, its ink browned with age, addressed in a careful hand to "whoever finds this place after me." Lina let out a breath that was half laugh, half sob. "He wasn't losing it," she said. "He was saving it."

When they brought the ledger to breakfast, the room fell utterly silent, and then everyone began talking at once. Jiddo looked at the bundle in Yusuf's hands, and for a moment the fog in his eyes seemed to lift completely. "I heard the rain," he explained simply, "and I could not let the water take it a second time." Yusuf read the letter aloud: it had been written by Jiddo's own father, thanking his son for his courage during the flood and urging him to remember that a family's true wealth lies in honesty, not pearls. Uncle Faisal was quiet for a long while after that. Then he stood up, walked out to the courtyard, and apologised to Hamid with a sincerity that nobody in the family would ever forget.

On Thursday, the curator arrived and handled the ledger as though it were made of glass, promising that it would be displayed beside the letter and the story of its hiding place. Jiddo insisted that the secret niche should be preserved rather than sealed, and he asked Hamid, of all people, to build a small cedar door to cover it. The carpenter accepted the work with a smile that said more than any words could have. That evening, Yusuf sat on the third step as the call to Maghrib drifted across the rooftops of Al-Balad. He had always imagined that mysteries were solved by unmasking a villain, but this one had no villain at all, only a frightened boy from long ago and an old man who had never stopped protecting what he loved. Sometimes, Yusuf thought, the answer is hidden in plain sight, waiting for someone patient enough to listen.

pages.text: In the oldest quarter of Jeddah, where coral-stone houses lean towards each other like elderly men sharing secrets, two rooftops face each other across a lane so narrow that a cat could leap from one to the other. Omar lived on the left side, and Rakan on the right, and for as long as either of them could remember, they had been inseparable. When they were eleven, bored during a long summer power cut, they had invented a code using nothing but two battered torches and a great deal of stubbornness. Long flashes, short flashes and carefully timed pauses could carry almost any message across the darkness. Their parents had assumed it was a phase that would fade, but five years later the lights still blinked between the two houses almost every night. By now the boys could hold entire conversations without saying a single word aloud.

Rakan lived with his grandfather, Jaddi Saleh, a quiet craftsman who repaired the carved wooden rawasheen that shaded the windows of the old houses. The workshop on the ground floor always smelled of sawdust and cardamom, and Omar had spent so many afternoons there that the old man treated him as a second grandson. 'A good lattice,' Jaddi Saleh liked to say, running his thumb along the delicate joints, 'holds together because every piece leans on another.' The boys would roll their eyes at this, having heard it a hundred times, but they never quite told him to stop. Each evening, after prayers and homework, they climbed to their rooftops and signalled the day's news: a teacher's terrible joke, a goal scored in the street, a plan for the weekend. It was, Omar would later realise, the steadiest thing in his life.

The trouble began in the autumn, when the regional robotics competition was announced. Omar and Rakan had been planning their entry for months, sketching designs on the backs of envelopes and arguing cheerfully over every gear and sensor. Then a group of older students from Omar's new school, who had won the competition twice before, invited him to join their team. Flattered and frankly dazzled, Omar accepted on the spot, and only afterwards did the weight of what he had done settle on his chest. Rather than face his friend, he sent a short message explaining that it was 'too good an opportunity to turn down'. The reply came within seconds and consisted of just two words: 'Go, then.' That night, for the first time in five years, the window across the lane stayed completely dark.

Weeks turned into months, and the silence hardened into something neither boy knew how to break. Omar shoved his torch into the back of a drawer, telling himself that he had outgrown childish games anyway. His new teammates were clever and confident, and the robot they built was undeniably impressive, yet working with them felt strangely hollow. Nobody laughed at his clumsy drawings or teased him when he got a calculation wrong; they simply corrected him and moved on. When they passed in the lane, Rakan would nod politely, which was somehow worse than if he had ignored Omar altogether. More than once, Omar found himself glancing at the dark window opposite before bed, half expecting a flicker that never came.

One sweltering night in early summer, a thick wall of dust rolled in from the desert, and shortly after midnight the electricity failed across the whole district. Unable to sleep in the airless heat, Omar climbed to the roof, hoping for even the faintest breeze. The city had vanished into a brownish haze, and the only light came from the occasional car crawling along a distant road. He was about to go back inside when something caught his eye: a weak, trembling glow in the window across the lane. Three short flashes, three long, three short, repeated over and over. Omar's breath caught in his throat, because he would have recognised that pattern anywhere.

He fumbled his way downstairs, tore open the drawer and dug out his old torch, praying the batteries had not died. When he flashed back the signal they had always used for 'I'm here', the reply came so fast that he almost dropped it. Slowly, letter by letter, he deciphered the message: 'JADDI FELL. CAN'T LIFT HIM. PHONE DEAD.' For a fraction of a second, an absurd thought crossed Omar's mind, that Rakan had not spoken to him in eight months. Then the thought evaporated, and he was hammering on his parents' door before he had even decided to move. 'Baba, wake up, it's Jaddi Saleh!' he shouted. His father, who had seen many emergencies in his years as a nurse, was pulling on his shoes before Omar had finished explaining.

They found the old man lying at the foot of the workshop stairs, conscious but grey with pain, while Rakan knelt beside him, gripping his hand. Omar's father examined him with calm, practised movements and announced that the hip was probably broken but that his breathing and pulse were steady. He called an ambulance on his own phone, then asked Omar to hold the torch steady so that he could see properly. In the circle of light, Rakan looked up, and for a long moment the two boys simply stared at each other. 'You answered,' Rakan whispered, as though he could hardly believe it. 'Of course I answered,' said Omar, and his voice cracked in a way he did not bother to hide.

The hospital corridor was cold and bright, and the boys sat side by side on hard plastic chairs while the doctors took Jaddi Saleh for an X-ray. For a while neither of them spoke, but eventually Rakan cleared his throat. 'I didn't really expect anyone to see,' he admitted. 'I just didn't know what else to do, so I kept flashing.' Omar stared at his hands and confessed that he had looked at Rakan's window almost every night since their quarrel. 'I was a coward,' he said quietly. 'I should have told you to your face, and I should never have abandoned our project in the first place.' Rakan gave a tired laugh and admitted that he had been checking Omar's window too, far too proud to be the one who blinked first.

By dawn, the doctors had confirmed a clean fracture that would heal well with surgery and patience. When the boys were finally allowed in, Jaddi Saleh was propped against his pillows, looking pale but distinctly pleased with himself. He studied the two of them standing together at the end of his bed and raised one bushy eyebrow. 'So,' he said, 'it took a broken old man to fix a broken friendship. I should have fallen down the stairs months ago.' The boys protested loudly, and he chuckled until the nurse warned him to rest. Before he closed his eyes, he murmured, 'Remember, a lattice holds because every piece leans on another,' and this time neither of them rolled their eyes.

A week later, with the electricity long restored and Jaddi Saleh recovering at home, Omar climbed to his rooftop just after the evening prayer. He had already told his teammates that he would help them prepare for the competition but would be entering next year with his original partner. Across the lane, a figure appeared, and a familiar light began to blink. Omar grinned as he decoded the message: 'NEW DESIGN. BETTER GEARS. YOUR DRAWINGS STILL TERRIBLE.' He flashed back a single word, the one they had always used to end their conversations, which meant something like 'always' in their private language. Then the two lights went on talking long into the night, steady and bright, two small stars hanging over the old city.

pages.text: Every morning in early spring, the clouds came down from the sky and walked through Grandfather Saleh's farm as though they owned it. Faisal had watched them all his life from the terraced slopes outside Abha, thick white fog drifting between the juniper trees, soaking his sleeves and beading on his eyelashes. Yet for all that moisture in the air, the ancient stone terraces below the house were cracking, and the coffee bushes his grandfather had tended for forty years were slowly losing their battle with the dry season. "The rain isn't what it used to be," Grandfather would say, running his weathered fingers over a brittle leaf. Faisal, sixteen and stubbornly practical, had never been one to accept a problem simply because it was old. Standing in the fog one morning, feeling it cling to his skin, a question struck him with almost physical force: what if the water they needed wasn't falling from the sky at all, but floating right in front of them?

That evening, Faisal buried himself in research papers until well past midnight. He discovered that in the coastal deserts of Chile and Morocco, villages had been harvesting fog for years using vast vertical nets made of fine plastic mesh. As fog passes through the mesh, tiny droplets collide with the fibres, merge together, and eventually grow heavy enough to trickle down into gutters below. Some installations were reportedly collecting hundreds of litres a day, enough to sustain entire communities. "It's almost too simple," he muttered, scribbling calculations in the margin of his notebook. His older sister Noura, who was studying statistics at university and rarely missed an opportunity to tease him, peered over his shoulder. "Simple ideas are usually the ones that either change everything or fail spectacularly," she said, "so you had better collect proper data if you want anyone to take you seriously."

When Faisal presented his proposal for the regional science fair, the reaction from his classmates was, to put it mildly, lukewarm. Turki, who had won the previous year with an elaborate solar-powered irrigation system, leaned back in his chair with an unmistakable smirk. "You're going to catch clouds with a fishing net?" he asked, and half the room burst out laughing. Faisal felt his cheeks burn, but before he could respond, their teacher, Ustadh Hamad, raised a hand for silence. "Every serious scientific idea sounds ridiculous to someone at first," he said calmly, "so the question isn't whether it sounds strange, but whether the evidence supports it." He agreed to supervise the project on one condition: Faisal had to design a rigorous experiment, with measurements taken every single day for six weeks.

Grandfather Saleh listened to the plan in thoughtful silence, sipping his cardamom-scented coffee, and Faisal braced himself for polite scepticism. Instead, the old man set down his cup and smiled in a way Faisal had not seen for months. "When I was a boy," he said, "my own grandfather used to leave flat stones beneath certain trees, and in the morning they would be wet even when no rain had fallen. We thought it was a blessing from Allah, and perhaps it was, but perhaps He also gave us minds to understand how it worked." Together they spent the following weekend building three collectors from wooden posts, sheets of double-layered mesh, and sections of plastic guttering salvaged from an old storeroom. They positioned them along the ridge where the fog was thickest, each one angled to face the prevailing wind. By sunset, Faisal's hands were blistered and his back ached, but he could hardly wait for morning.

The first dawn was a revelation. Faisal ran up the slope in the half-light, his breath forming small clouds of its own, and found clear water dripping steadily from the gutters into the containers below. He measured the contents with trembling hands: just under four litres from the first collector, a little over three from the second, and almost five from the third. It was hardly enough to revive a whole farm, yet it was undeniably real, water drawn from what had seemed like empty air. Noura, who had insisted on joining him, recorded every figure alongside the temperature, humidity, and wind speed. "Don't get carried away," she warned, though she was grinning too. "One good morning is an anecdote, not a result."

The second week brought a setback that nearly ended everything. A violent storm swept in from the west one night, and by morning two of the three collectors lay flattened in the mud, their mesh torn to shreds and their posts snapped like matchsticks. Faisal stood among the wreckage, utterly deflated, unable to speak for several minutes. "Perhaps Turki was right," he finally admitted, kicking at a broken gutter. "Perhaps this was a fantasy all along." Grandfather Saleh placed a heavy hand on his shoulder and said nothing for a while, gazing out at the valley. "These terraces were built stone by stone by men who watched floods wash away their work a hundred times," he said at last. "They did not give up, so neither will you."

Rather than simply rebuilding, Faisal decided to treat the disaster as data. He analysed the damage and realised that the rigid frames had acted like sails, catching the full force of the gusts until something had to give. Working late into the evenings, he redesigned the collectors with flexible joints and tension cables anchored deep into the rocky soil, allowing the structures to bend without breaking. He also experimented with a tighter mesh weave after reading that smaller gaps could capture finer droplets, a modification that turned out to be crucial. Ustadh Hamad visited the farm to inspect the new design and nodded approvingly. "Failure is simply information you haven't learned to use yet," he remarked. When the next storm arrived ten days later, all three collectors swayed and creaked, but every one of them was still standing at dawn.

By the end of the six weeks, the notebook was crammed with figures, and Noura spent an entire weekend transforming them into graphs. The results exceeded even Faisal's most optimistic predictions: the redesigned collectors averaged nearly eleven litres each per foggy morning, more than double the yield of the original models. Noura also uncovered a striking pattern, showing that the highest yields occurred when the wind blew steadily from the southwest at moderate speeds. "You see?" she said, tapping the screen. "This isn't luck, it's a predictable relationship, which means you could position future collectors far more efficiently." Faisal stared at the neat lines climbing across the chart and felt something shift inside him. For the first time, he truly understood that science was not about being right at the start, but about being honest enough to keep testing until the truth revealed itself.

At the regional science fair, Faisal's stand was modest compared with the gleaming robots and elaborate screens around it: just a scaled-down collector, a misting machine borrowed from a garden centre, and Noura's carefully printed graphs. Yet as the morning progressed, a crowd gradually gathered, and the judges lingered far longer than he had dared to hope. One of them, an environmental engineer from a university in Jeddah, questioned him relentlessly about mesh density, maintenance costs, and how the system might be scaled across the mountainous south. Faisal answered every question, admitting openly where his knowledge ran out. When the results were announced that afternoon, his project was awarded first prize, and the engineer invited him to visit her research laboratory during the summer holidays. Turki was among the first to approach him afterwards, and to Faisal's surprise, he extended his hand. "I owe you an apology," he said sheepishly, "and honestly, I'd love to know whether my solar pumps could move your water uphill."

Months later, on a cool morning when the fog lay thick across the valley, Faisal and his grandfather walked together along the terraces. Water from a row of twelve collectors now flowed through a network of pipes into a small stone reservoir, and from there to the roots of the coffee bushes, which had begun to put out glossy new leaves. Turki's solar pump hummed quietly beside the tank, the two rivals having become, somewhat unexpectedly, firm friends and collaborators. Grandfather Saleh stopped beside a bush heavy with young green berries and cradled one gently in his palm. "My grandfather's wet stones were the beginning of an answer," he said softly, "and you have finished the sentence he started." Faisal looked up at the clouds drifting through the junipers, no longer seeing them as something that merely passed by. They were, he realised, a gift that had been waiting patiently all along for someone curious enough to catch it.

options: The mesh was too fine to let water through
Their rigid frames caught the full force of the storm winds
Turki damaged them out of jealousy

options: They were unenthusiastic about the idea

questions.q: What did Noura mean when she said, 'One good morning is an anecdote, not a result'?
options: Faisal should write a story about his experiment
The water from the first morning was not clean
A single success is not enough evidence to prove anything

questions.q: What pattern did Noura discover in the data?
options: Yields were highest during heavy rainstorms
Yields were highest with steady southwest winds at moderate speeds
Yields were the same regardless of the weather

questions.q: What can we infer from Grandfather Saleh saying Faisal had 'finished the sentence' his own grandfather started?
options: He sees Faisal's project as continuing and explaining traditional knowledge
He wants Faisal to stop experimenting
He believes the old methods were completely wrong

pages.text: Faisal had spent most of his sixteen years believing that the Empty Quarter was simply a blank space on the map, a place people mentioned only to illustrate the idea of nothingness. So when his uncle Majid, a geologist at the university in Riyadh, invited him on a research trip to the Wabar craters, he accepted mainly because it would make an impressive story at school. What he hadn't bargained for was his grandfather insisting on coming along. "I crossed those sands before your uncle was born," the old man announced at dinner, in a tone that made it clear the matter was closed. Faisal exchanged a doubtful glance with his uncle, but neither of them dared to argue. Grandfather's eyesight was no longer what it had been, yet his stubbornness, it seemed, had only grown sharper with age.

They set off before dawn, the four-wheel drive loaded with water, fuel and enough scientific equipment to fill a small laboratory. Faisal sat in the back with a satellite navigation device on his knees, tracking their progress with the quiet satisfaction of someone who trusts technology completely. Every so often, Grandfather would lean towards the window and murmur something about the shape of a dune or the direction its ridges were facing. "The wind writes on the sand every night," he said, "and anyone who can read it will never be lost." Faisal smiled politely, though privately he considered such advice charmingly outdated. After all, why would anyone need to read the wind when a satellite could tell you your position to within three metres? He would later look back on that thought with considerable embarrassment.

By early afternoon, they had reached the craters, a series of shallow hollows half-swallowed by the restless sand. Scattered across the ground were glossy black fragments that glittered in the harsh light like broken pieces of night. "Impact glass," Uncle Majid explained, crouching to pick one up. "When the meteorite struck, the heat was so intense that it melted the sand instantly." Grandfather nodded slowly and told them that, according to the old stories, a proud city had once stood here before fire fell from the sky. Faisal pointed out that scientists had dated the impact to only a few centuries ago, and that no city had ever been found. "Perhaps," Grandfather replied with a faint smile, "but a story doesn't have to be true about the past to be true about people."

It was Grandfather who noticed the change first, long before any of the instruments did. The air had grown unnaturally still, and on the southern horizon a dull brown haze was creeping upwards like smoke from a distant fire. "We need to secure everything now, not in ten minutes," he said, and for once nobody questioned him. They had barely managed to pack the equipment and shelter inside the vehicle when the storm hit with a roar that drowned out all conversation. Sand hammered against the windows so fiercely that Faisal half expected the glass to crack. For hours they sat in the stifling darkness, sipping water sparingly and listening to the desert rage around them. Somewhere in the middle of the night, exhausted by fear as much as by heat, Faisal finally drifted into an uneasy sleep.

When dawn came, the silence was almost more unsettling than the storm had been. Forcing open the door, they discovered that sand had piled up against one side of the vehicle, burying the wheels almost to the axles. Worse still, the satellite phone, which had been strapped to the roof rack, had vanished entirely, and the navigation device refused to switch on. "The battery must have overheated," Uncle Majid muttered, shaking it as though that might somehow bring it back to life. While digging out the rear wheel, he stepped awkwardly into a hollow and twisted his ankle so badly that he could barely put any weight on it. Faisal felt his stomach tighten as the reality of their situation sank in. They were in the middle of the largest sand desert on earth, with no map, no signal and only one driver who could still use both feet.

"You'll have to drive," Uncle Majid said quietly, handing Faisal the keys. Faisal had practised in the desert near their farm, but never in terrain like this, and he was painfully aware that a single mistake could leave them stranded for good. It took the three of them over two hours to free the vehicle, with Uncle Majid hopping between the wheels to lay down the metal boards and Grandfather directing the work as calmly as if he were organising a family picnic. When at last the engine growled and the tyres gripped the sand, Faisal let out a breath he hadn't realised he'd been holding. "Good," said Grandfather, settling into the front passenger seat. "Now, if you're willing to listen to an old man's outdated advice, I'll take you home." Faisal had the grace to blush, and he didn't argue.

Grandfather couldn't see the dunes clearly, so he asked Faisal to describe them in detail: which side was steep, which side was gentle, how the ripples curved across the surface. From these descriptions he pieced together the direction of the prevailing wind and, from that, the route they needed to follow. "Keep the long slopes on your right," he instructed, "and never try to climb a slip face, however tempting the shortcut looks." Twice Faisal was convinced they were heading the wrong way, and twice he bit his tongue and trusted the old man's judgement. Gradually, he began to notice patterns he had been blind to only a day earlier, as if someone had quietly translated the landscape into a language he could understand. By late afternoon, he was reading the sand almost before Grandfather asked him to.

Just as the sun was beginning to sink, a deep, low hum rose from somewhere ahead of them, so powerful that Faisal felt it vibrating through the steering wheel. He slammed on the brakes, convinced that something had gone terribly wrong with the engine. Grandfather, however, laughed out loud for the first time since the storm. "That's the singing dune," he said, his voice thick with emotion. "I heard it when I was younger than you, travelling with my father's caravan, and I never thought I'd hear it again." Uncle Majid explained that when sand of exactly the right size slides down a dune, the grains vibrate together and produce a sound like a distant engine or a deep musical note. To Faisal, though, the scientific explanation did nothing to diminish the wonder of it. More importantly, Grandfather now knew precisely where they were: the old caravan track lay less than a night's drive to the north.

Driving through the desert at night was a risk, but with their water supply running dangerously low, waiting until morning was hardly an option. Grandfather told Faisal to look for al-Jadi, the star that never moves, which travellers have used to find the north for thousands of years. Faisal found it with surprising ease, a steady point of light hanging above the darkness like a promise. Mile after mile, he kept it framed in the top corner of the windscreen, adjusting his course whenever the dunes forced him to swerve. Uncle Majid dozed fitfully in the back, his ankle propped up on a bag, while Grandfather recited verses of poetry under his breath to keep Faisal awake. Never in his life had Faisal concentrated so hard, nor felt so strangely calm.

Not long before dawn, a flicker of orange appeared on the horizon, and Faisal's heart leapt into his throat. As they drew closer, it turned out to be a campfire belonging to a family of camel herders who had pitched their tent beside the track. Without asking a single question, the herders welcomed them in, poured them bitter cardamom coffee and pressed handfuls of dates into their hands. One of the young men had a working phone, and within minutes Uncle Majid was reassuring his anxious wife that they were safe. The eldest herder listened to the story of the storm and then turned to Faisal with an approving nod. "You drove by the stars," he said. "Your grandfather has taught you well." Faisal glanced at Grandfather, who was pretending, quite unsuccessfully, not to look proud.

Back in Riyadh a week later, Faisal stood in front of his class to present his project on the Wabar craters. He described the meteorite, the impact glass and the physics of the singing dune, but he also told them about reading the wind and steering by al-Jadi. "I used to think that science and tradition were rivals," he concluded, "but out there I learnt that they're really two ways of paying attention to the same world." That evening, Grandfather called him into the majlis and placed a small piece of black glass in his palm. "I picked this up at the craters," he said, "so that you would never forget the night you learnt to see." Faisal turned it over in the lamplight, watching it gleam like a fragment of the desert sky. He knew, with absolute certainty, that he never would.

His grandfather asked him to drive.

options: Fires lit by the people of a lost city

questions.q: In the story, what does the word 'stifling' (page 4) suggest about the inside of the vehicle?
options: It was hot and difficult to breathe in.

questions.q: Why was the singing dune so important to their journey?
options: Its sound scared away the sandstorm.

options: He decided that technology is useless in the desert.
He no longer wanted to study science.
He came to respect traditional knowledge alongside science.

pages.text: Every family has a secret-keeper, and in the Al-Rashid household that role belonged to a grey parrot named Mishmish. Mishmish had a genius for mimicry that bordered on the supernatural. He could reproduce the microwave's beep, the doorbell's chime and every voice in the house with alarming accuracy. Sixteen-year-old Yousef had long suspected that the bird listened to every conversation and stored it away for later use. So when his father announced that his new manager, Mr. Al-Hamdan, was coming to dinner on Thursday, Yousef's first thought was not about the food. It was about the parrot.

For three days, the house was gripped by preparation. His mother was meticulous, polishing glasses that were already spotless and arranging the cushions in the majlis with almost scientific precision. His father, meanwhile, rehearsed his small talk in front of the hallway mirror, completely unaware of his feathered audience. "Mr. Al-Hamdan, what an absolute honour to have you in our home!" he declared, before frowning and shaking his head. "No, too much. He'll think I'm trying too hard." From his cage in the corner, Mishmish tilted his head and absorbed every syllable.

On Thursday afternoon, his father took Yousef aside with the seriousness of a general briefing a soldier. "Your mission is simple," he said. "The parrot stays in your room, the cover stays on the cage, and nobody hears a single word from him." Yousef saluted and named it Operation Silence. Within twenty minutes, however, the doorbell rang, and his father rushed to the door, straightening his thobe, only to find an empty street. When it happened a second time, and then a third, Yousef crept upstairs and discovered Mishmish under his cover, chiming away with obvious satisfaction.

When the real guest finally arrived, he turned out to be every bit as dignified as his reputation suggested. Mr. Al-Hamdan was a tall, silver-bearded man who, according to office legend, had never once smiled during a meeting. He greeted everyone with formal politeness, accepted his coffee and dates, and settled into the majlis with an expression that gave absolutely nothing away. The kabsa was steaming, the conversation was polite, and for nearly half an hour everything went according to plan. Yousef was just beginning to relax when he noticed that his seven-year-old sister, Lulwa, was missing. He also noticed, with a sinking feeling, that she had taken a handful of dates with her.

He reached the top of the stairs just in time to see a grey blur shoot past his ear. "He looked hungry!" Lulwa protested, standing beside the open cage with a date in her hand. Yousef hurtled back down the stairs, but he was far too late. Mishmish had already swept into the majlis and perched himself on the curtain rail directly above the guest of honour. The entire room fell silent as the bird looked down at the stern visitor, puffed up his chest and cleared his throat in a perfect imitation of Yousef's father. Then, in that same unmistakable voice, he announced: "Mr. Al-Hamdan, what an absolute honour to have you in our home! No, too much. He'll think I'm trying too hard."

His father turned the colour of a ripe tomato, and Yousef wished the floor would swallow him whole. Unfortunately, Mishmish was only warming up. He produced the shriek of the smoke alarm, which had gone off that afternoon when the first batch of sambousa had burned to a crisp. Then, switching effortlessly to his mother's voice, he whispered in a conspiratorial tone: "Don't tell anyone they're from Abu Saleh's bakery." His mother froze with the serving plate still in her hands, the incriminating sambousa arranged on it in a flawless circle. It was, Yousef reflected, the most thorough sabotage he had ever witnessed, and it had been carried out by a creature with a brain the size of a walnut.

Desperate to end the catastrophe, Yousef grabbed a towel and made a heroic leap towards the curtain rail. Mishmish simply hopped to the bookshelf, and Yousef landed awkwardly on a cushion, sending a bowl of pistachios scattering across the carpet. Lulwa giggled, his mother groaned, and his father looked as though he was calculating how quickly he could update his CV. Through all this chaos, Mr. Al-Hamdan sat perfectly still, his face completely unreadable. Then Yousef noticed that the man's shoulders had begun to shake. For one horrifying moment, he thought their guest was furious, until a deep, rumbling sound escaped him and Yousef realised, to his astonishment, that the man was laughing.

It was not a polite chuckle but a full, helpless laugh that brought tears to his eyes. "Forgive me," Mr. Al-Hamdan gasped, wiping his face with a handkerchief. "I have a cockatoo at home called Sultan, and he is a criminal of exactly the same kind." He went on to explain that Sultan imitated his ringtone so convincingly that he answered imaginary phone calls several times a day. Worse still, the bird had learned to say "Just five more minutes" in his voice, which he had apparently mumbled every morning when his alarm went off. "Last month," he admitted sheepishly, "Sultan said it loudly during a video call with the entire department, and I have never fully recovered my dignity."

After that confession, the atmosphere in the room transformed completely. The careful, rehearsed conversation disappeared, and in its place came stories about mischievous pets, disastrous dinners and childhood mishaps. Mishmish, sensing that he was no longer in disgrace, eventually fluttered down and settled comfortably on Mr. Al-Hamdan's shoulder. Yousef's mother, recovering her composure, offered the guest more sambousa with a rueful smile. "Abu Saleh makes the best in the city," Mr. Al-Hamdan said in a deadpan voice, taking two. "You made an excellent choice." His laughter turned out to be contagious, and soon even Yousef's father was laughing so much that he had to put down his coffee.

On Sunday evening, his father came home from work with news. Mr. Al-Hamdan had put him in charge of the company's most important new project. "He told me that anyone who can keep calm with a parrot like ours can handle any client in the world," his father said, shaking his head in disbelief. The whole family cheered, and Lulwa insisted that Mishmish deserved a reward. Yousef had to admit that Operation Silence had been the most successful failure of his life. As if he had been following the conversation, Mishmish ruffled his feathers and spoke up from his cage in a perfect imitation of Yousef's own voice: "Mission complete. Nobody heard a single word."

options: Lulwa was ringing the bell as a joke
He was expecting a delivery from the bakery

options: Yousef forgot to close the cage

What secret did Mishmish reveal about the sambousa?

questions.q: Why was Mr. Al-Hamdan's reaction to Mishmish probably so different from what the family expected?
options: He had not heard what the parrot said

He wanted to buy the parrot from them

pages.text: The sun had barely cleared the sandstone cliffs of AlUla when Faisal began brushing the dust from Najma's grey coat. The mare stood perfectly still, her ears flicking towards every distant sound, as though she already knew what the day held in store. 'She's calmer than you are,' his grandfather observed, leaning on his walking stick at the edge of the makeshift stable. Faisal managed a nervous laugh, for his stomach had been tying itself in knots since the call to Fajr prayer. Forty years earlier, his grandfather had ridden Najma's great-grandmother across these same valleys, and the family had been breeding endurance horses ever since. 'Remember the only rule that matters,' the old man said quietly. 'In this sport, the horse runs the race, and the rider simply has the honour of keeping her company.'

Endurance riding, Faisal had often tried to explain to his classmates, was nothing like the thundering sprints they saw on television. The junior race covered eighty kilometres of desert, divided into loops, and after each loop every horse had to pass through a 'vet gate', a strict veterinary inspection. Within twenty minutes of arriving, a horse's heart rate had to drop below sixty-four beats per minute, or it would be eliminated on the spot, no matter how far ahead it had been. Consequently, the fastest horse rarely won; victory belonged to the rider who could read his animal best. Across the paddock, Faisal spotted Rakan, his long-standing rival, surrounded by a team of grooms in matching jackets. Rakan's chestnut stallion, Barq, had been imported from Europe at enormous expense, and Rakan had made no secret of the fact that he expected to win by a comfortable margin.

When the starting flag dropped, more than thirty horses surged forward in a cloud of golden dust. Every instinct in Faisal's body urged him to chase the leaders, yet he deliberately held Najma back to a steady, rhythmic trot. Rakan swept past him within the first kilometre, glancing over his shoulder with a grin that was almost a challenge. 'Let him go,' Faisal muttered, more to himself than to the mare. He had learned the hard way, two years before, what happened to riders who bit off more than they could chew in the opening stages: their horses arrived at the first vet gate with hearts pounding like drums and never left it. So he kept his eyes on the track, his hands soft on the reins, and his breathing slow, until patience began to feel like second nature.

At the first vet gate, Faisal leapt down, loosened Najma's girth and poured cool water over her neck while his cousin Saleh held the bucket. Within four minutes, the veterinarian lowered her stethoscope and nodded approvingly. 'Fifty-six,' she announced. 'An exceptional recovery.' A few metres away, however, the atmosphere was considerably tenser, because Barq's heart rate was refusing to settle and his grooms were working frantically around him. 'Hurry up!' Rakan snapped at them, pacing back and forth as the minutes ticked by. Eventually the stallion passed, but only narrowly, and Faisal noticed that Rakan's confident grin had been replaced by a tight, anxious frown.

The second loop wound through a maze of narrow canyons, where towering rock formations cast long shadows across the soft sand. By the halfway point, Faisal realised with a jolt of excitement that he had overtaken nearly everyone, and only Rakan remained somewhere ahead. Najma was moving beautifully, her stride smooth and unhurried, as if she had been saving her strength precisely for this moment. For the first time, Faisal allowed himself to picture the trophy glinting in his grandfather's majlis. He could almost hear the congratulations, the phone calls from relatives, the photograph in the local newspaper. Then, rounding a sharp bend, he heard something that made his blood run cold: the high, panicked scream of a horse.

Barq was standing riderless on a slope of loose sand, trembling, his reins tangled around one foreleg. Below him, Rakan lay half-propped against a boulder, his face pale and his left ankle twisted at an unnatural angle. 'He stumbled in the deep sand,' Rakan gasped. 'I tried to stay on, but I came off badly.' Faisal glanced back along the trail; there was no sign of a marshal, and his phone showed no signal whatsoever between the steep canyon walls. He knew perfectly well that every minute he spent here would hand the race to someone else. Yet he also knew that a frightened horse with its legs caught in the reins could break a bone in a single wrong step.

Without allowing himself to dwell on the consequences, Faisal dismounted and approached Barq slowly, murmuring the same soothing words his grandfather used with nervous foals. The stallion snorted and rolled his eyes, but gradually he lowered his head, and Faisal managed to free the tangled reins. Next, he gave Rakan his water bottle and used the emergency whistle on his saddle, blowing three long blasts that echoed off the rocks. It felt like an eternity before two marshals on quad bikes finally roared into view, although it had been barely fifteen minutes. As they lifted Rakan onto a stretcher, he caught Faisal's sleeve. 'Why did you stop?' he asked, his voice barely above a whisper. 'You could have won this.' Faisal shrugged. 'Some things are more important than winning,' he replied, and he realised, to his surprise, that he genuinely meant it.

By the time Faisal remounted, three riders had already passed him, and the temptation to make up the lost ground at a reckless gallop was almost overwhelming. Instead, he forced himself to keep a level head, because Najma had stood in the heat for a long time and her muscles would need several kilometres to warm up again. He spoke to her softly, felt for any hesitation in her stride, and let her choose a pace she could sustain. In the final stretch, the first three horses were neck and neck, racing flat out towards the line, while Faisal and Najma followed at a controlled canter. They crossed the finish in fourth place, to a polite ripple of applause. Faisal felt a pang of disappointment, but when he patted Najma's damp neck, she turned her head and nudged him gently, as if to reassure him that all was well.

The final veterinary inspection was the most thorough of the day, and two of the top three horses struggled to pass, one showing signs of exhaustion and the other a slight lameness. Najma, by contrast, trotted up and down the inspection lane as though she had merely been out for a morning stroll. That evening, the organisers gathered everyone for the prize-giving ceremony beneath strings of warm lights. After presenting the main trophies, the chief steward cleared his throat. 'The Best Condition Award recognises the horse finishing in the finest health, and therefore the rider who cared for it most wisely,' he declared. 'This year, it goes to Najma, ridden by Faisal Al-Harbi, who, we have been informed by our marshals, also stopped mid-race to help a fellow competitor.' The applause that followed was far louder than anything he had heard at the finish line.

Afterwards, his grandfather held the small silver plate up to the light, and Faisal noticed that the old man's eyes were glistening. 'I have won many races,' his grandfather said, 'but this is the prize I would have wanted most.' Just then, Rakan limped over on crutches, his ankle heavily bandaged and his usual swagger nowhere to be seen. 'I owe you an apology, and a thank-you,' he said awkwardly. 'Perhaps next season we could train together, if you'd be willing to teach me how you keep Najma so calm.' Faisal smiled and held out his hand, and Rakan shook it firmly. Above the dark cliffs, the first stars appeared, and as Najma rested her head on Faisal's shoulder, he could feel her heartbeat: slow, steady and strong.
