options: He was secretly disappointed that Faisal did not win first place
He believed only winning first place truly mattered
He valued care for the horse and good character more than victory

stories.title: The Boy Who Helped Measure the Earth

pages.text: In the spring of the year 1020, the fortress of Nandana stood on its ridge like a stone crown, overlooking a plain so flat that it seemed to have been ironed by the hand of the wind. Yusuf, a sixteen-year-old copyist from Ghazni, had been sent there with a single instruction from his uncle: make yourself useful to the scholar, and do not ask foolish questions. The scholar in question was Abu Rayhan al-Biruni, a man whose reputation had travelled further than most caravans. He was said to know the movements of the stars as well as a shepherd knows his flock. Yusuf had expected someone grand and remote. Instead, on his first morning, he found a thin, sun-darkened man crouching on the battlements, squinting at the horizon as though it owed him money.

"Tell me, young man," al-Biruni said without looking up, "how large do you suppose the Earth is?" Yusuf hesitated, aware that his uncle's warning about foolish questions presumably applied to foolish answers as well. "The scholars of Baghdad measured it, I believe," he ventured. "In the days of the Caliph al-Ma'mun, they walked across the desert counting their steps." Al-Biruni smiled, clearly pleased. "They did, and it was a magnificent effort, but it required dozens of men, months of walking and a desert as level as a tabletop. I intend to do it with one mountain, one instrument and, if you prove reliable, one assistant."

The instrument was an astrolabe, a disc of polished brass engraved with lines so fine that Yusuf hardly dared to breathe near it. Over the following days, al-Biruni explained his plan, sketching triangles in the dust with the end of his staff. First, they would determine the exact height of the hill beside the fort by measuring its peak from two different points on the plain. Then they would climb to the summit and measure how far the horizon dipped below a perfectly level line. "Because the Earth is round," he said, tapping the sketch, "the horizon falls away from us, and the higher we stand, the further it falls." Yusuf stared at the drawing until, quite suddenly, the idea fell into place like a key turning in a lock. If you knew the height and the angle, geometry would do the rest.

Not everyone at the fort shared his enthusiasm. A visiting official named Hamid, who had a habit of laughing at his own jokes before anyone else could, made no secret of his scepticism. "You cannot measure the whole world from a hilltop," he scoffed over dinner. "One might as well weigh the sea with a teaspoon." Al-Biruni merely dipped his bread in the lentils and replied that a teaspoon, used patiently and with good arithmetic, could tell you a surprising amount about the sea. Yusuf, however, lay awake that night turning Hamid's words over in his mind. What if the scholar was mistaken, and he, Yusuf, had spent the whole spring carrying instruments up a hill for nothing?

The measurements of the hill's height took the better part of a week. Each morning they set out before dawn, while the air was still and the distant peak stood sharp against the sky, and each afternoon Yusuf copied the figures into a leather-bound notebook. Twice al-Biruni made him repeat a calculation because a single digit had been carelessly written. "An error the width of a hair here," he warned, "becomes an error the width of a province by the time we reach the end." By the time they had finished, Yusuf's fingers were stained black with ink and his patience had been stretched almost to breaking point. Yet he had also begun to notice something unexpected: he was enjoying himself.

On the morning they were due to climb to the summit, a dust storm rolled in from the west and swallowed the plain whole. The horizon, which they so badly needed, simply vanished behind a wall of yellow haze. For three days they waited, and with every passing hour Hamid grew more insufferable. "Perhaps the Earth has heard of your plan and is hiding," he chuckled. Yusuf felt his temper rise, but al-Biruni placed a calm hand on his shoulder. "Patience is half of knowledge," he said quietly, "and the other half is knowing when to use it." They prayed the dawn prayer together on the fourth morning, and when they stepped outside, the sky was as clean as freshly washed glass.

The climb was steeper than Yusuf had anticipated, and by the time they reached the top he was gasping, with the precious astrolabe wrapped in cloth and clutched against his chest. Below them, the plain stretched out in every direction, and far away the land met the sky in a thin, trembling line. Al-Biruni set up the instrument with the care of a jeweller, adjusting it again and again until he was satisfied that it was perfectly level. Then he sighted along the brass arm towards the horizon and held his breath. For a long moment, neither of them spoke. At last he read out the angle, a tiny fraction of a degree, and Yusuf wrote it down with a hand that was not entirely steady.

That evening, by the light of a single oil lamp, they worked through the calculation together. Al-Biruni had already worked out the method, but he insisted that Yusuf follow every step himself, explaining that knowledge borrowed is never quite as secure as knowledge earned. The numbers grew longer and more stubborn, and more than once Yusuf had to go back and find where he had gone astray. Shortly before midnight, he reached the final line and looked up, almost afraid to speak. "If I have done this correctly," he said, "the radius of the Earth is a little over three thousand two hundred and eighty miles." Al-Biruni checked the figures in silence, then nodded slowly, and something like joy flickered across his tired face.

When they compared their result with the one reached by the scholars of al-Ma'mun's age, the two figures turned out to be remarkably close. Hamid, to his credit, had the grace to admit he had been wrong, although he did so in a voice so low that it was almost drowned out by the clatter of plates. "A teaspoon after all," he muttered, and for once he did not laugh at his own joke. Yusuf could not help grinning. What struck him most was not that the measurement had worked, but how simple it had been once someone had dared to think about the problem differently. The whole round world, it seemed, had been hiding inside a single angle all along.

Al-Biruni later recorded the method in his writings, and nearly a thousand years afterwards, scholars would marvel at how close his figure came to the measurements made with satellites. Yusuf's name never appeared in those pages, but he did not mind in the least. He returned to Ghazni at the end of the summer with an ink-stained notebook, a sunburnt neck and a new habit of looking at every horizon as though it were a question waiting to be answered. When his uncle asked whether he had made himself useful, Yusuf thought for a moment before replying. "I think," he said, "the scholar made me useful to myself." And from that day on, he never again believed that any question was too large to ask.

options: The height of the hill and the angle at which the horizon dipped
The number of steps across the desert and the position of the stars
The distance to Baghdad and the length of a shadow at noon

options: Hamid refused to let them leave the fort
A dust storm hid the horizon

Why did al-Biruni insist that Yusuf follow every step of the calculation himself?
options: He was too tired to do it himself
He wanted to test whether Yusuf was lying
He believed knowledge you work out yourself is more secure

options: He regretted spending the summer at Nandana
He had discovered his own abilities and curiosity
He planned to become an official like Hamid

pages.text: The email arrived on a Thursday evening, and Layan read it three times before she dared to believe it. Out of more than four hundred applicants, she had been chosen as one of six finalists in the Junior Kitchen Challenge, which would be filmed live in Riyadh the following month. For the final, each contestant had to prepare a dish that told the story of their family, and Layan knew at once what hers would be: her grandmother's saleeg, the creamy rice cooked slowly in chicken broth and milk that had filled every family gathering she could remember. There was only one problem, and it was a considerable one. Her grandmother had never written the recipe down. The only record was a battered notebook in which, beside the word 'saleeg', someone had scribbled a single mysterious line: 'Stir until it sings.'

That weekend, Layan's father drove her up the winding mountain road to Taif, where her grandmother lived surrounded by rose bushes and an alarming number of cooking pots. 'How much rice, Yumma?' Layan asked, her pen hovering over a fresh page. Her grandmother laughed and cupped her hands together. 'This much, habibti, or a little more if your uncles are coming.' When Layan pressed her about the cooking time, the old woman merely tapped her ear and said, 'You don't watch the clock, you listen to the pot.' Layan smiled politely, but inwardly she groaned, because the judges would hardly be impressed by a contestant who claimed her rice had been cooked according to its mood.

Back in Jeddah, she turned the family kitchen into something resembling a science laboratory. She weighed every grain of rice, measured the broth to the millilitre and recorded each attempt in a spreadsheet, convinced that precision would succeed where tradition had failed. Her younger brother, Saad, became her official taster, a role he accepted with suspicious enthusiasm. The first batch was so watery that he asked whether it was meant to be soup, and the second had stuck so badly to the pan that their mother had to soak it overnight. By the fifth attempt, however, Layan had finally produced something edible by following a strict schedule on her phone's timer. 'It's good,' Saad admitted, chewing thoughtfully, 'but it isn't quite Yumma's.' Layan pretended not to hear him, although the comment lodged itself in her mind like a splinter.

The studio in Riyadh was a far cry from her mother's cosy kitchen. Six gleaming workstations stood beneath blinding lights, each equipped with an induction hob, a digital oven and a screen displaying the countdown. At the station beside hers stood Reem, a self-assured girl from Dammam who had brought her own probe thermometer and spoke about cooking temperatures as though she were reciting poetry. 'Saleeg?' Reem said, raising an eyebrow when Layan explained her dish. 'Brave choice. It's very easy to overcook rice.' The head judge, Chef Hamad, a tall man famous for his honesty, welcomed them with a warning: 'In a kitchen, things rarely go according to plan, and the best cooks are the ones who adapt.' Little did they know how soon his words would be put to the test.

When the countdown began, Layan felt her nerves give way to a calm sense of purpose. She browned the chicken with cardamom, cloves and a stick of cinnamon, and the warm, sweet aroma instantly reminded her of Taif. Following her carefully planned schedule, she added the rice to the simmering broth and set her timer for exactly eighteen minutes. Across the studio, the other contestants were chopping, whisking and plating with impressive speed, while the cameras glided silently between them. Everything was going perfectly, which, as Layan would later reflect, should have been her first warning sign.

Without warning, a deafening crack of thunder shook the building, and a second later the entire studio was plunged into darkness. Gasps echoed around the room as the hobs fell silent and the countdown screens went blank. Within a minute, the emergency lights flickered on, casting a dim orange glow over the anxious faces of the contestants. Chef Hamad's voice rose calmly above the confusion: 'The storm has knocked out the power, but the competition continues. We have portable gas burners, and you will have whatever time remains.' The technicians hurried in with small camping stoves, and Layan realised with a sinking feeling that her schedule had become worthless. A gas flame would heat her pot in an entirely different way, and her phone, which she had left in her locker, could no longer save her.

For a moment, Layan stood frozen, staring at the pot as if it might offer her instructions. Then, almost without thinking, she heard her grandmother's voice: 'You don't watch the clock, you listen to the pot.' She lowered the flame, began to stir slowly and, ignoring the bustle around her, closed her eyes. At first the liquid bubbled quickly and noisily, with a thin, splashing sound. Gradually, as the rice released its starch and she added the warm milk little by little, the bubbling grew deeper and softer, until it became a gentle, rhythmic 'blup... blup...' that sounded almost like humming. Her eyes flew open, and she very nearly laughed out loud, because she finally understood what 'until it sings' had meant all along.

Glancing sideways, Layan noticed that Reem was in trouble. Her thermometer had been knocked onto the floor in the darkness and had shattered, and she was staring helplessly at a pan of butter, unsure whether her sauce was ready. Layan hesitated for only a second before leaning over. 'Listen to it,' she whispered. 'When the butter stops crackling and goes quiet, and it smells like toasted nuts, it's done.' Reem looked doubtful, but she bent closer to the pan, and moments later her face lit up with relief. 'Thanks,' she murmured, and for the first time all day, she didn't sound in the least superior. When the bell finally rang, both girls were plating their dishes with only seconds to spare.

The judging took place under the emergency lights, which somehow made the moment feel even more dramatic. Chef Hamad lifted a spoonful of Layan's saleeg, studied its glossy, velvety texture and tasted it in silence that seemed to last an eternity. 'Your cooking time on a stove you had never used was flawless,' he said at last. 'How on earth did you manage it without a timer?' Layan took a deep breath. 'I didn't time it, Chef. I listened to it, the way my grandmother taught me, although it took me a month and a power cut to understand what she meant.' The chef put down his spoon and, to everyone's surprise, smiled broadly. 'That,' he said, 'is the difference between following a recipe and actually knowing one.'

When Chef Hamad announced that Layan had won, the studio erupted in applause, and Reem was the first to hug her. Later that night, still clutching her trophy, Layan called her grandmother, who had watched the entire final on television, the storm included. 'I heard it, Yumma,' Layan said, her voice trembling. 'I heard the pot sing.' There was a pause, and then her grandmother chuckled softly. 'Then now you know the recipe, habibti, and nobody can ever take it away from you.' Back at the hotel, Layan opened the battered notebook and, beneath that mysterious line, added a few words of her own: 'No timer needed. Just listen, and be patient.'

questions.q: Why was Layan's grandmother's recipe difficult to follow?
options: It was written in an old dialect that Layan could not read.
It contained no exact measurements or cooking times.
It required ingredients that were only available in Taif.

questions.q: What does the phrase 'a far cry from' mean in the sentence 'The studio in Riyadh was a far cry from her mother's cosy kitchen'?
Why did Layan's carefully planned schedule become 'worthless' after the power cut?
options: The judges had shortened the competition time.
She had forgotten which ingredients she had already added.
The gas burner would heat the pot differently, and she no longer had her timer.

questions.q: What can we infer about Layan's character from the way she helped Reem?
options: She wanted to impress the cameras and the judges.
She was generous and valued fairness over simply winning.
She believed Reem's dish had no chance of beating hers.

questions.q: What did Layan finally understand about the line 'Stir until it sings'?
options: It referred to the changing sound of the bubbling rice as it became ready.
It was a reminder to sing while cooking to stay relaxed.
It meant the rice should be stirred for exactly eighteen minutes.
